Single acting shock absorbers provide damping only during spring rebound, while double acting shock absorbers provide damping both during spring deflection as well as during rebound. Single acting shock absorbers do not generate damping force during spring deflection, which can lead to stiffer springs and a slight preload on the suspension spring due to the shock absorber return spring. In contrast, double acting shock absorbers allow for the use of softer suspension springs and provide optimal damping in both directions [2].

Damping on rebound only forces the use of stiffer springs due to their design. Single acting shock absorbers provide damping only during spring deflection, not during rebound [1]. This results in a requirement for softer suspension springs to achieve optimal damping in both directions [2]. The disadvantage is that this arrangement can interfere with the impact-isolating properties of the spring during its compression stroke, leading to undesirable downward acceleration when hitting a hole. To mitigate this, double acting shock absorbers are used which provide damping during both spring deflection and rebound, allowing for softer suspension springs and better overall performance [3].

A clutch-type no-spin differential stops one wheel from spinning uncontrollably by using friction clutches to lock the axles together whenever one drive wheel experiences uncontrolled slippage. This is described in [2] where it states that the multiple plate clutch type uses four side gear pinions on two shafts at right angles to each other, engaging similar V-shaped slots in the differential case. Each side gear is backed by a series of multiple disk clutches. When one wheel turns faster than the others, the faster-turning splined side member and driven clutch member cause the ramps on the center cam and driven clutch member cam to push the driven clutch member away from the spider. This action is similar to that described for other no-spin differentials.

The relationship between indicated horsepower (IPH) and brake horsepower (BHP) can be understood from [2] and [3]. In [2], it states that "Given the brake-horsepower formula" and provides a formula where torque is substituted for length of arm times scale reading, leading to a direct torque-horsepower-speed relationship. This implies that as torque increases with engine speed, so does indicated horsepower.

In [3], there's an explanation about overall efficiency which involves calculating BHP from IPH using the formula:

\[ \text{Brake horsepower} = \frac{\text{Work output in Btu's}}{\text{Fuel input in Btu's}} \times 100\% \]

This indicates that BHP is derived from IPH, showing a direct relationship where an increase in IPH results in an increase in BHP. However, it also mentions that the actual power at the crankshaft (BHP) is always less than the power produced within the engine (IPH), due to frictional losses and other mechanical inefficiencies.

Therefore, indicated horsepower is higher than brake horsepower because of the additional losses not considered in calculating BHP from IPH.

When using a hot gas bypass valve, if the coil temperature reaches the proper level, the switch closes to engage the clutch in the compressor. This engagement of the clutch results in the compressor running constantly (when it is activated) in the hot gas bypass valve system [2]. As the compressor runs continuously, the high-pressure gas from the compressor joins with the low-pressure gas exiting the evaporator. These two gases mix, causing a pressure increase and an increase in the boiling point of the refrigerant. This loss of cooling efficiency causes the evaporator temperature to increase, thus eliminating freezeup [2].
